This page contains information on how discounts and refunds should be
treated in the data.The statistical agency should examine the treatment
of discounts and refunds and assess their impact if possible (see for
example Ref.
[\[](https://www.ons.gov.uk/economy/inflationandpriceindices/articles/researchintotheuseofscannerdataforconstructingukconsumerpricestatistics/2021-04-06)[1](https://www.ons.gov.uk/economy/inflationandpriceindices/articles/researchintotheuseofscannerdataforconstructingukconsumerpricestatistics/2021-04-06)[\]](https://www.ons.gov.uk/economy/inflationandpriceindices/articles/researchintotheuseofscannerdataforconstructingukconsumerpricestatistics/2021-04-06)).

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Treatment of discounts {#Treatmentofdiscountsandrefunds-Treatmentofdiscounts}

In general, prices obtained from scanner data (or web scraped data)
should be consistent with the price concept used in the CPI. For
example, they should include any taxes and charges that are directly
connected to the purchase of the priced product.

In addition to conceptual considerations, the treatment of discounts is
very much dependent on the way that discounts are recorded in the
data. There can be different types of discounts. For example:

- Temporarily reduced prices available to all consumers (for example 20%
  off). An average transaction price calculated over the reference
  period would cover both discounted and regular prices.
- An additional quantity in the product (for example 20% more weight).
  Such types of discounts may be linked to changes in the article codes.
  Linking or grouping techniques may be needed to properly capture these
  discounts (see [Identifying unique
  products](https://unstats.un.org/wiki/display/GWGSD/Identifying+unique+products)).
- Lower prices for damaged or defective products, or products close to
  their expiry date. It could be argued that such price reductions
  should not be included in the CPI given these are not products of
  comparable quality, but it may not always be possible to identify such
  transactions separately in the data.
- Clearance prices for products reaching the end of their product
  lifecycle - the [Dumping filter](dumping-filter.qmd) can
  help identify these cases when expenditure information is available.
- Loyalty cards and loyalty refunds. Very often, information on such
  schemes cannot be extracted from the scanner data.
- Multibuy offers (for example 'Buy 2 get 1 for free\'). Such schemes
  may or may not be captured in the turnover and sales data for a
  specific article. Depending on the recording of such transactions, the
  average price may or may not be lower than the price charged for a
  single article.  

It is very important to discuss these aspects with the data supplier
where possible (see section [Data requirements specification for scanner
data](data-requirements-specification-for-scanner-data.qmd)).

# Treatment of refunds {#Treatmentofdiscountsandrefunds-Treatmentofrefunds}

Refunds happen when consumers return the product that they have
previously purchased. Such transactions are typically treated as
negative sales by the retailers. Depending on the data set, returns may
or may not be separately identifiable. They can be included in the
turnover and sales data of an article code. Turnover and sales could (in
theory) become negative, in which case they should best be removed.
Refunds may also be shown separately in the data. A further complication
is that refunds may be recorded in a period other than the period of
purchase. Refunds could play a more important role in some product
categories, such as clothing, and may be less common in other product
categories, such as food.

# Other considerations {#Treatmentofdiscountsandrefunds-Otherconsiderations}

Deposits should be excluded from the price used in the calculations. The
articles in the scanner data or web scraped data that have a deposit
should be identified and the deposit fee should be deducted from the
price where applicable.

With web scraped prices, delivery charges or credit card fees may apply.
The treatment of such additional costs is discussed in paragraphs
11.78-11.80 of the [CPI
Manual](https://www.imf.org/-/media/Files/Data/CPI/cpi-manual-concepts-and-methods.ashx).

For a review of how discounts and refunds could be treated in scanner
data please see Ref. (1).
